Definition: Whether the scheme rules governing payment system participation, pricing structure, technical requirements, security standards, and conduct are publicly accessible via website, public repository, or on request. Transparency indicator.
Comments: Searched BoT site and public web for a public TIPS scheme rulebook/rules document (‘TIPS rulebook’, ‘scheme rules’, ‘operating rules’) but did not find a publicly posted rulebook; working paper notes “scheme management functions include operating rules” but does not link to a public rules document. Value set to unknown due to lack of direct evidence of public availability.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Row was scored 0/Unknown with no cited source. A single light-check search surfaced the AfricaNenda State of Inclusive Instant Payment Systems (SIIPS) 2024 Tanzania case study, an authoritative and directly on-topic source, so the row was escalated from the fast path to the full path. The case study states TIPS scheme rules are available to participants and non-participants upon request (not freely published online), while the Bank of Tanzania website separately hosts downloadable copies of the National Payment Systems Act 2015, the Payment Systems Licensing and Approval Regulations 2015, and the TACH and TISS rules. Recalculated from 0 to 2 (Partial - On Request) rather than 3 (Fully Public), since the TIPS-specific rulebook itself is not confirmed to be freely downloadable.
revised_comments: The Tanzania Instant Payment System (TIPS), operated by the Bank of Tanzania, is governed by the TIPS Rules 2024, which set out participation, operating and conduct requirements. According to the AfricaNenda State of Inclusive Instant Payment Systems in Africa 2024 Tanzania case study, these scheme rules are made available to both participants and non-participants upon request, rather than being freely published online. Related payment system instruments, including the National Payment Systems Act 2015 and the TACH and TISS rules, are downloadable from the Bank of Tanzania website.

Definition: Whether digital payment systems and access points (apps, USSD, agents) are designed to accommodate persons with disabilities (visual, hearing, mobility, cognitive impairments), and disability-disaggregated coverage rates if data available.
Comments: Searched for explicit national payment accessibility requirements for persons with disabilities (e.g., regulations mandating accessible ATMs/USSD/assistive tech). Tool results mainly show media reporting barriers rather than policy mandates. No credible regulatory evidence found; value unknown.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light check surfaced a peer-reviewed 2025 article (Ally, African Disability Rights Yearbook) that is directly on topic, so the row was escalated to the full path. Evidence is genuinely mixed: a Tanzania Bureau of Standards specification (DTZS 6/3227) sets general ICT accessibility requirements applicable to self-service transactions, but the peer-reviewed article concludes there is no binding legal requirement mandating accessible design specifically for FinTech/mobile money platforms, and that accommodations for persons with disabilities remain voluntary and unevenly implemented. Because the two sources point in different directions and neither gives a clean fit to the 1/2/3 scale, this is flagged for human review rather than upgraded on a single interpretation.
revised_comments: Tanzania has general disability-rights protections, including the Persons with Disabilities Act 2010, the National Policy on Disability 2004 and constitutional non-discrimination guarantees, alongside a Tanzania Bureau of Standards specification (DTZS 6/3227) setting ICT accessibility requirements for self-service transactions. However, no legislation or regulation specifically mandates that digital payment systems and access points accommodate persons with disabilities, and accessibility features in mobile money and payment platforms are largely voluntary and unevenly implemented.

Definition: Percentage of government payments (G2P disbursements including salaries, pensions, social transfers) made through instant digital payment system rather than cash or check, reflecting government adoption and modernization.
Comments: Searched for quantified share of government payments digitized in Tanzania (e.g., % of G2P/G2G digital) via World Bank/BoT sources; no credible percentage evidence located in tool outputs. Value set to unknown.
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Light check surfaced a 2025 government/UN conference presentation citing 62% of TASAF (Productive Social Safety Net) beneficiaries paid via mobile money and 36% via bank account, an authoritative-looking figure, so the row was escalated to the full path. However, a 2024 World Bank PSSN II supervision document and a 2026 peer-reviewed study (Nyaki, Nystrand and Mwinuka) both indicate an over-the-counter cash option remains in use and that beneficiary adoption of digital payment 'remains limited', with cash still the most preferred method for many recipients. None of the sources quantify digitisation across the full G2P scope defined by this variable (salaries, pensions and social transfers combined), nor confirm the use of the instant/TIPS payment rail specifically rather than ordinary bank transfer. Given conflicting figures and incomplete scope coverage, this is flagged for human review rather than scored on the 1-5 scale.
revised_comments: Tanzania's flagship social transfer programme, the Productive Social Safety Net (PSSN/TASAF), pays beneficiaries electronically via mobile money or bank account, alongside a residual over-the-counter cash option; a 2025 government presentation reports 62% of beneficiaries paid via mobile money and 36% via bank account, though independent research suggests actual beneficiary adoption of digital payment channels remains uneven. Beyond this social-transfer scheme, no consolidated data on the share of all government payments (including salaries and pensions) made through Tanzania's instant payment system could be identified.
